scores.values_concern: The 'cold flat, no car, no one nearby' picture is invented colour; keep to the area-level finding and avoid a stereotyped image of poorer patients.
scores.accuracy_concern: Deprivation is measured by area (deprivation fifth), not personal income; adjusted odds ratios of about 1.15 to 1.19 are modest and the absolute gap may be only a few percentage points; the data are 2004 to 2011 and cover England and Wales; the link does not show that the pathway itself produces the gap.
scores.sharpen: Get the absolute 30-day and 1-year figures by deprivation fifth from the full text and lead with them as 'N in 100', dropping the invented scenario.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check whether the Haj-Mirzaian 39% is the prevalence of occult fracture on advanced imaging or of fractures needing surgery, and state that it applies only to people selected for MRI or CT; NICE's trigger is fracture still suspected after normal X-rays, not inability to bear weight as such.
scores.sharpen: Name the trigger as NICE does (fracture still suspected after normal X-rays) and add the words a care worker or relative can use when the person is sent back still unable to stand.

scores.accuracy_concern: Predicted mortality by band must come from the published equation or validation tables, and the constants were recalibrated as mortality fell (Moppett 2012 and later); the premise that the score is used to decide against surgery needs a source or softer wording.
scores.sharpen: Show two icon arrays (a middle and a high band) so readers see that most people in high bands survive 30 days, and cite how the score is actually used in decisions.

scores.values_concern: Uses an audit indicator as the foil: keep to published NHFD wording and imply nothing about Scottish Hip Fracture Audit findings or design.
scores.accuracy_concern: Upright minutes (57.6 versus 45.1) are day-4 means from one Norwegian trial of a geriatric ward model; confirm the exact wording of the mobilisation indicator before contrasting with it.
scores.sharpen: Pair the day-4 upright minutes with a practical ward measure a team could record (times out of bed per day) and keep C03-23 from repeating the same trial.

scores.accuracy_concern: The practice finding rests on one small retrospective Sydney cohort (92 people); 'no one was offered food or drink' must not be generalised beyond that hospital; the ESA limits are for elective anaesthesia and the Sip til Send consensus source is still unlocated.
scores.sharpen: Find a UK or multi-centre fasting audit to sit beside the Sydney cohort and lead with the one practical change: restart fluids when an operation is postponed.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check NICE CG124 wording (the original text says 'consider adding nerve blocks' rather than 'offer'); a single-shot block lasts hours, so 'spares pain at every later move' overstates; in UK practice the block often follows X-ray confirmation, so the drawn sequence must match that.
scores.sharpen: Say how long a single block usually lasts so the timing argument stays accurate, and give families the exact question: has a nerve block been offered?

scores.accuracy_concern: The 34% comes from one Australian orthogeriatric unit with formal swallowing assessment; the link with pneumonia and death is observational and must be 'linked with'; the list of warning signs still needs an RCSLT or NICE source.
scores.sharpen: Say who can do a bedside swallow screen on an orthopaedic ward, and make the family action concrete: sit the person upright and watch the first cup.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'The one trial' of outreach rehabilitation in care homes is probably an overclaim; that staff-continued rehabilitation would keep the gains is an inference, not a tested finding.
scores.sharpen: Drop 'the one trial', open on the 4-week gain that faded when visits stopped, and turn the handover diagram into three things a care home can ask the ward for.

scores.accuracy_concern: The Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 is only partly in force, so avoid stating the NI process; in Scotland a welfare attorney or guardian with medical treatment powers can consent, not only be consulted; statutes, codes and GMC guidance need opened copies, not web pages.
scores.sharpen: Keep the nation-by-nation detail in the source reply and build the caption around one question: what would she want, and who is making this decision?

scores.accuracy_concern: There are no data on how many hip fracture patients are carers, as the candidate notes; census figures need an opened ONS or NRS document; the Carers (Scotland) Act emergency planning provision needs checking; the problem applies to any emergency admission, so hip fracture is the example, not the claim.
scores.sharpen: Name a same-day route that exists (ward social work, a local carer centre's emergency line) so the request leads somewhere.

scores.accuracy_concern: Levy 2021 has not been read; persistent opioid use after hip fracture (Danish cohort) is unverified; the link between opioids and falls is observational.
scores.sharpen: Read Levy 2021 and quote its discharge recommendation, and add the one line the discharge letter should tell the GP.

scores.accuracy_concern: Magaziner's cohort was community-dwelling people in Baltimore in 1990 to 1991; times to maximum recovery are group averages and many people never regain earlier function; the UK discharge-guidance claim is unverified and official pages could not be opened.
scores.sharpen: Give the family the words to use ('Can we decide after rehabilitation, or after a supported trial at home?') and verify the discharge-guidance line or drop it.

scores.accuracy_concern: The 22% and 36% are shares of all exclusions, not the share of patients excluded, and readers will misread them; the 'over 40% have dementia' figure is Cochrane background and needs a primary source; consultee rules differ between England and Wales and Scotland.
scores.sharpen: Replace 'share of exclusions' with the proportion of trials that excluded people with dementia, which readers grasp at once, and consider moving it to C20.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check that 'decreased in most' is the authors' wording and whether a UK series is included; the near doubling by 2050 is a projection that assumes current rates and population forecasts.
scores.sharpen: Use the UK line from Sing 2023 if it exists and end with the reading habit: ask whether a figure is a rate or a count.

scores.accuracy_concern: Morrison and Siu data are from 1990s New York and may not describe current practice; Ruel 2021 is small and retrospective; the '83% of cognitively intact patients had no standing order' figure needs checking against the abstract.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the protocol finding rather than 25-year-old US data, state plainly that the data are old, and keep clear of the earlier pain-in-dementia posts.

scores.accuracy_concern: The opening says abilities come back 'at very different speeds', but the trousers (about 20%) and stairs (about 90%) figures are new dependence at a time point, so they describe whether an ability returns, not how fast; the cohort dates from 1990 to 1991.
scores.sharpen: Rewrite the opening to match the data (how many people regain stairs compared with dressing) and run it only if C03-12 does not use the same Magaziner timeline.

scores.accuracy_concern: HIP ATTACK secondary outcomes (less delirium and pain, earlier mobilisation) favoured accelerated surgery, so the post must say it did not reduce deaths or major complications, not that speed has no benefit; the observational delay figures are associations.
scores.sharpen: Add one line on the secondary outcomes so the post can't be read as 'speed doesn't matter', and close on the concrete target: surgery on the day of or the day after admission.

scores.accuracy_concern: The primary outcome is a composite (death or inability to walk about 3 metres at 60 days); about 16% crossed from spinal to general; the population was previously ambulatory patients in the US and Canada; families inform the choice rather than make it.
scores.sharpen: Say what the trial did not settle (people with advanced dementia, longer-term outcomes) and give families one question to ask the anaesthetist.

scores.accuracy_concern: The gait study had only 16 older patients; the NSQIP association is likely confounded by fracture pattern and fixation (restriction is prescribed for harder cases), so 'linked with' only; the BOAST or NICE full weight-bearing wording is unverified.
scores.sharpen: Add what restriction means for the patient (not walking, or walking in breach) and one question a physiotherapist can put to the surgeon.

scores.accuracy_concern: UK guidance (NICE NG24) uses 70 g/L, or 80 g/L with acute coronary syndrome, not the FOCUS 80 g/L threshold; the trial is from 2011 and most UK practice has already moved; the result must not be extended to people with acute myocardial infarction.
scores.sharpen: Align the threshold with UK guidance and say what a symptom trigger means at the bedside, so the post adds something to what most readers already do.

scores.accuracy_concern: NICE CG124 frames the list as comorbidities to identify and treat immediately so that surgery is not delayed, not as reasons that justify delay; the antiplatelet and echocardiography advice must be checked in the Griffiths 2021 full text; DOAC timing varies with drug and kidney function.
scores.sharpen: Keep NICE's framing (treat these immediately so they don't delay surgery) and add who to ask about DOAC timing.

scores.values_concern: Caution, not disqualifying: the post must not suggest that dementia, frailty or care home residence alone justifies not operating; keep surgery as the default and non-operative care as a narrow, discussed choice with active palliative care.
scores.accuracy_concern: FRAIL-HIP was not randomised (people chose); the 83% 30-day mortality without surgery reflects who chose it near the end of life and must not be read as the effect of not operating; quality of life was proxy-rated; the 'quality of dying' figure needs checking.
scores.sharpen: Show what care without an operation involves day by day, and say near the top that this was a small non-randomised group who chose.

scores.accuracy_concern: Trondheim tested admission to a geriatric ward with comprehensive geriatric assessment, which differs from UK orthogeriatric co-management on an orthopaedic ward; the SPPB difference of 0.74 on a 0 to 12 scale needs a plain reading.
scores.sharpen: Merge with C03-04, or open on the four-month walking result in plain words rather than on the trial design.

scores.accuracy_concern: Single-centre, open trial in women only from the early 2000s; a mortality difference this large has not been a consistent finding in later nutrition trials and the Cochrane review rates certainty low, so the limitation must sit beside the mortality result.
scores.sharpen: Put the limitation in the same sentence as the mortality result and show the energy difference as an everyday food equivalent.

scores.accuracy_concern: EQ-5D data at 4 months were available for only 71.6%, largely because of deaths and missing responses; the post should say how the trial addressed the intraoperative cement reaction rather than leaving it out.
scores.sharpen: Frame it for families and GPs as why most half hip replacements now use cement, or leave it to orthopaedic accounts.

scores.accuracy_concern: A subgroup of a 1990s Finnish trial with very small moderate-dementia groups; 'living independently' is place of residence at 3 months; the Cochrane review rates the evidence low or very low.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the mild-dementia result, print group sizes, and add two adaptations (repetition, familiar staff) a family can ask for.

scores.accuracy_concern: Evidence on how often hip pain is felt in the knee is thin (one descriptive injection study and case reports); the anatomy needs a textbook source; no frequency should be given.
scores.sharpen: Combine with C03-02 as a two-part 'missed hip fracture' carousel, or keep to a sourced anatomical diagram and one examination habit.

scores.accuracy_concern: The difference (22.9% versus 17.8%) was not statistically significant, so the wording must be 'did not show a clear difference'; participants were a select group still not walking in daily life at enrolment.
scores.sharpen: Explain an active control in one sentence and close on the realistic point that many people need more than 16 weeks.

scores.values_concern: Criticises what hip fracture audits report; Alasdair chairs the Scottish Hip Fracture Audit, so the post risks implying his view of audit design or unpublished audit findings.
scores.accuracy_concern: The NHFD already collects 120-day follow-up on mobility and residence, so 'rarely followed after discharge' may be wrong for UK audit; Griffiths 2015 is a qualitative study of 31 people and supports a priority, not a measure.
scores.sharpen: Check what the NHFD reports at 120 days before contrasting, and centre the post on the patients' priority rather than on audit design.

scores.accuracy_concern: The links between low mood or fear of falling and slower recovery are observational; the Lenze and Visschedijk sources are unverified; the Bower 2020 trajectories come from one US cohort.
scores.sharpen: Make it specific to hip fracture with the fear-of-falling trajectory figures, give the one question to ask at the 6-week review, and check it against the C01 fear-of-falling candidates.

allocation_reason: About 15 distinct candidates score 44 or more on checkable trial or guideline evidence with no disqualifying flag; 13 takes the strongest without two posts on one trial or cohort (Trondheim, Magaziner) or a run of near-identical trial-result icon arrays, and the earlier set already had 20 hip fracture posts.
balance_note: The top 13 split 5 public (C03-12, 22, 02, 09, 18), 3 both (06, 07, 14) and 5 practitioner (17, 21, 19, 04, 03), which is balanced. Most are teaching or explanation rather than complaint. Two series are missing from the top 13: Care that works (best candidates C03-24, 26) and Who gets left out (C03-10, 01). Swapping C03-03 or C03-18 for C03-24 or C03-10 would cover them at little cost in score. Also watch format: 17, 18, 20, 25 and 28 all use trial-result icon arrays, so no more than two of them should run. Note: the weights as given sum to a maximum of 55, not 50.
